Financial planning · Access to money · Visual planning guide

Who can pay the next bill? Draw an account-access plan beside the balance sheet

Use four charts to distinguish cash owned from cash an authorized payer can use, then stress a temporary access delay against the daily payment calendar.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore an interruption in access to household money

Interactive planning lab

Extra opening cash needed before any payment event$1,000
Existing cash unavailable to the bill payer at the start$12,000
Operating cash after 60 days$10,000

Hypothetical 60-day access interruption. Opening cash is already usable by the person legally authorized to make the modeled payments. A separate existing cash balance becomes usable at the start of the selected day; this is a transfer of existing household resources, not income. Living costs leave daily at the monthly input divided by 30. Income arrives only at the end of days 30 and 60, after that day’s costs. Cash earns zero interest. Negative values are unfunded payments, without automatic borrowing or bill deferral. The assumed release date does not establish legal authority, document validity, account ownership or an institution’s processing time. Existing authority and actual access must be confirmed separately.

The central idea

A household may own enough money and still face an earlier payment gap. Record access, authority and timing alongside every balance assigned to essential bills.

01

Begin with the person who must make the payment

A balance sheet records ownership and debt. A payment plan also needs to identify who can give an instruction, which account they can use and when the funds become accessible. These questions can matter during an illness, an absence or an interruption in normal account access.

The Government of Canada’s financial power-of-attorney overview distinguishes authority to manage someone’s property from ownership of that property. It also explains that document names and requirements vary across provinces and territories. A financial model cannot establish that a document or proposed instruction is valid.

The calculator starts after that separate authority check. Its opening amount means money already usable by the authorized bill payer. Its delayed balance means existing household cash that becomes usable on an independently assumed date. That date is a stress input, rather than a bank processing standard or a legal deadline.

02

Give the opening and delayed balances different roles

The example has CAD 2,000 accessible at the start and a separate CAD 12,000 balance awaiting access until day 21. The household owns CAD 14,000 across these two balances. Only CAD 2,000 can fund a payment before the second amount becomes usable.

The first chart shows those two balances and their labelled total. Do not add the total bar to its components. Releasing CAD 12,000 later changes where the money can be used; it does not create CAD 12,000 of earnings, a gift or an investment gain.

An actual access record should avoid storing login credentials, passwords or verification codes. Record the institution, the account’s purpose, the person’s confirmed role and the institution’s process for giving authorized instructions. Keep sensitive account details in a private location appropriate for the people who need them.

03

Find the shortage before the delayed money arrives

Living costs are CAD 4,500 per thirty-day period, allocated at CAD 150 a day. Before the start of day 21, twenty daily amounts have left: 20 × CAD 150 = CAD 3,000. Against CAD 2,000 initially available, that creates a CAD 1,000 funding gap.

The separate CAD 12,000 arrives before day 21’s spending. Net income of CAD 2,500 arrives after spending on days 30 and 60. Those later receipts improve the account balance, but cannot make the earlier payments without another resource. The graph retains within-day payment points rather than showing only a reassuring month-end amount.

The comparison grants access to the same separate balance at the start of day 1. Both paths use identical assets, income and expenses. Their difference is timing. Neither path assumes an overdraft, a bill extension or an automatic transfer from some unlisted account.

04

Reconcile the end without losing the access problem

After sixty days, the example has received all CAD 12,000 of delayed cash and two CAD 2,500 income payments, and has paid CAD 9,000 of living costs. The ending balance is CAD 2,000 + CAD 12,000 + CAD 5,000 − CAD 9,000 = CAD 10,000.

That positive endpoint coexists with the earlier CAD 1,000 shortage. All allowed access dates occur within sixty days, so changing the date preserves the endpoint while potentially changing the minimum balance. The waterfall reconciles the total resources; the daily line answers whether those resources arrive in time.

The matrix varies access dates and spending. Its values show additional opening cash beyond the amount already entered. A zero cell covers the selected simplified calendar. It does not establish a complete emergency reserve or a probability that an institution will process an instruction by that date.

05

Review the access plan when circumstances change

  1. Identify the essential bills and their actual payment dates.
  2. Confirm who is authorized to give instructions for each intended resource.
  3. Ask the institution what documents and procedures apply to that role.
  4. Test a delay without assuming that another account or credit facility is available.
  5. Keep a current, private record that an authorized person can locate.

A joint account and an authority to act for another person have different ownership and responsibility implications. The government’s overview discusses both. Use the arrangement that has been properly established for the circumstances; this calculator neither selects an arrangement nor grants access.

This is a living-household cash exercise. Death, estate administration, beneficiary payments and estate authority require a separate plan. The estate-liquidity article covers the related timing question without treating the two situations as interchangeable.
